newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels take lenient view of past misdeeds.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels take lenient view of past misdeeds.

text.p: As they relentlessly wrest territory from President Mobutu Sese Seko, Zaire's rebels insist there will be no sweeping penalties for past misdeeds.

"We consider we are all virgins. We are all blank sheets of white paper," said Yagi Sitolo, one of the rebels' new provincial governors. "We are starting from zero. Those who do not do a good job in future will be punished," he said in Kisangani, a diamond town which fell to the rebels on March 15.
The rebels now control nearly half of Africa's third-largest country and entered Zaire's second city Lubumbashi on Wednesday.
Yagi was explaining why Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) has re-instated most of the corrupt regime's former officials in "liberated" areas.
Ordinary people are quietly elated by the transformation in Kisangani since the arrival of the rebels.

Residents stroll down the dirty boulevards late into the night when the air is cool. Before March 15 streets were deserted after dusk except for Mobutu's lawless soldiers and the foreign mercenaries recruited against the rebels.
The soldiers looted just before they fled but for at least the past 15 years soldiers and police throughout Zaire extorted money and goods from civilians on a routine basis.

"Before the Alliance came there were five road-blocks on this stretch and we would have paid something at every one of them," said Alois, a 66-year-old retired salesman, during a drive this week 50 km (30 miles) south of Kisangani. There was not a single rebel soldier in sight.
Government officials were as venal as the men in uniform. For every service, citizens paid a fee, which was immediately pocketed. When no fee existed, the officials made one up.
"Today, a head of department dare not even accept a glass of Coca-Cola," said Governor Yagi.
"The example has to be given by us, the leadership. I can assure you that it was the first time a new governor was not sent cases of beer by the brewery or showered with gifts."
Following the pattern in other towns seized by the rebels, only very senior Mobutu officials fled with those foreign and local residents most heavily implicated in corruption.
Many of these prominent supporters are from Mobutu's small tribe from northwest Zaire, the Ngbandi.

Security chiefs and most of the feared Special Presidential Division (DSP), a 10,000-strong force trained by Israelis, are Ngbandi. They know the rebels will not be as lenient with them as with the others who served Mobutu.
The DSP men in Lubumbashi put up strong resistance.
Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 but has seen his hold over the sprawling country crumble as rebels advance, announced a state of emergency on state television late on Tuesday.

He appointed military governors to areas not under rebel control and the capital Kinshasa, where shots rang out on Wednesday as security forces tried to break up a march by supporters of new prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi.
The rebels know that if they punished all those who were corrupt the entire apparatus of the state would be unmanned. But not everyone likes this approach.
"People who really ruined things have to be put out of harm's way," said Ndomba Benda, a university professor.
"If you keep the same people, those with minds anchored in the past, there will be problems," he said.
Mobutu's officials were paid peanuts if at all and Ndomba, a 51-year-old with two masters' degrees from British universities who earns $26 a month, says that has to stop.
Governor Yagi agrees he has quite a job on his hands.
"We need to change people's minds. We have lived for 32 years in a system where anti-values like theft and corruption became values."

The change will not happen overnight. Zaireans, or Congolese as those in Kabila's area are now called, are used to living by Article 15, a fictitious clause in the constitution which advises people to grab what they can.
Emerging from a meeting with the senior Alliance official in Kisangani, a visitor was taken to one side by a man lounging in the ante-chamber.
"Look, I've got 100 grammes of very good gold from Kilimoto mine. Can I bring it around to show you?" the man inquired.
